1254.title: Life without principle
1254.hook: he warns against spending life only to earn a living (Life Without Principle)
1254.howItsDone: Some readers of Life Without Principle take from it a habit of setting aside time for something done for love rather than pay, as a check on letting work fill the whole of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Cape Cod: a book that opens with a wreck and ends with all America at Thoreau's back. Your line was the indifferent sea.

Two men in the same woods. One walks there half of every day because he loves them. The other spends his whole day cutting them down for profit. Which one does the town respect? Thoreau poses almost exactly that question, and answers it: the walker gets called a loafer, and the man clearing the woods, industrious and enterprising. He isn't telling a joke. He's opening an essay about what a society rewards, and what it quietly calls a waste of time.
screen: `TWO MEN IN THE WOODS.` → `A LOAFER, AND AN ENTERPRISING CITIZEN.` → `WHAT DOES A TOWN REWARD?`

segments.voice: First, the bustle. The essay is called Life Without Principle, and one of its plainest lines is this: "This world is a place of business. What an infinite bustle!" He says the noise of it wakes him at night. Trains, trading, hurry; work everywhere, and almost no talk about why. Second, the loafer and the citizen. His point isn't that work is bad. It's that a life gets measured by what it earns, so the person who loves the woods looks idle and the one who strips them looks useful. Third, hire for love. Don't hire someone who does your work only for the money, he says; hire the one who does it for love of it. Pay matters, but a worker's aim should be to do a certain work well, not only to get a living from it. Fourth, more than a living. The heart of the essay is a worry: that people spend the whole of life getting a living, and never get around to living. Earning money isn't the enemy. Rent is real, and Thoreau took paid work himself, surveying land among other jobs. But he asks whether anything in your days is something money didn't buy and couldn't: a walk, a friendship, a song you sing to nobody. It's an uncomfortable essay that doesn't let anyone off easily, its author included. But the question at its center is simple to carry: what in your life is more than a living?

segments.voice: Let your work, paid or unpaid, settle at the edge of your mind, and ask: what's one thing that earns nothing, done just because it's good? A walk without a step count, a call to an old friend, ten minutes with a book or a guitar or a garden. Let one thing come, and picture yourself in it.

1255.title: The journal
1255.hook: he kept a journal, mostly about the woods
1255.howItsDone: People who borrow Thoreau's habit often keep a nature journal, a short daily note about weather, plants or birds they saw, which trains the eye as much as the hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was life without principle: Thoreau's warning about a life spent only getting a living. Your line was more than a living.

"Do you keep a journal?" That, more or less, is what a friend asked Thoreau. Some readers take the friend to be Emerson; the entry doesn't name him. The journal's very first entry records the question and says, in effect: so I make my first entry today. No grand plan, no vow. A friend asked, and he started. That small beginning became a habit, and the habit became the place where much of his life as a writer actually happened.
screen: `DO YOU KEEP A JOURNAL?` → `SO HE STARTS, THAT DAY.` → `A SMALL BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: First, the start. Not a revelation in the woods; a friend's question, and a decision to begin the same day. Second, what fills it: weather, birds, the color of a leaf, the sound of ice, a neighbor met on the road. Thoughts about books and God and politics are there too, but again and again the pages return to the woods, fields and rivers near Concord. It's a record of noticing. Third, the quarry. Readers who compare the journal with his books find early versions of passages that later went into them. It wasn't a diary of feelings so much as a workshop. He walked, he looked, he wrote it down, and some of it became Walden. Fourth, the line a day. You don't need his hours or his talent to borrow the habit. The journal's gift is that it makes you look. If you know you'll write one line tonight about something you saw outside, you go through the day a little more awake, searching for it: a cloud, a crow, the smell after rain. The line might be clumsy. That doesn't matter; the looking already happened. Thoreau kept his going and going. Yours can be a single sentence in a notebook or a note on your phone, as long as it's true and about something you actually saw.
screen: `A FRIEND'S QUESTION.` · `A RECORD OF NOTICING.` · `THE WORKSHOP FOR THE BOOKS.` · then, large: `ONE LINE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Go back over the last day and look only for something from nature: light on a wall, a bird you half heard, the air when you stepped out. Let one come forward without judging whether it's good enough. Then, silently, say it in one plain sentence: not pretty, true.
The journal. The notebook Thoreau began because a friend asked, and filled, page after page, with the woods. Today's word.
Your line: one line a day. The looking matters more than the writing. Until tomorrow.

1256.title: Seasons in the journal
1256.hook: late in life he tracked when each plant flowered, records some scientists still use
1256.howItsDone: Some people keep a seasonal record in Thoreau's spirit, noting the dates when one tree leafs out, flowers or turns color, which ties them to one place across the years.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the journal: the notebook Thoreau began because a friend asked. Your line was one line a day.

In Walden's chapter on spring, Thoreau does something a poet usually wouldn't. He lists dates: not of his own life, but the days the ice on Walden Pond broke up, year after year, so he could compare. In the middle of a rapturous chapter about thawing sand and returning birds sits a little column of records. The same man who wrote about sucking out the marrow of life also wanted to know exactly when the pond let go of winter.
screen: `A LIST IN THE SPRING CHAPTER.` → `WHEN THE ICE BROKE UP.` → `POET AND RECORD-KEEPER.`

segments.voice: First, the habit in Walden. "I have travelled a good deal in Concord," he wrote, half joking: Concord was his home town. He traveled deep instead of far, and part of that was writing down when things happened: the ice, the first birds, the frogs. Second, the habit grows. In his later journal the noting turns into lists and tables: when this plant leafed out, when that one flowered, when a bird first sang, season after season in the same fields. The poet's eye becomes a careful observer's, and he doesn't seem to think of those as enemies. Third, a notebook's long reach. His records have found readers he couldn't have pictured. Some people who study the seasons have gone back to them to compare flowering times then and now. A man noting a violet in a field near Concord left something useful to strangers far ahead of him. Fourth, records as practice. Keeping a record sounds dry. But to know when the maple turns, you have to look at the maple every day. Records are attention that has been kept, not thrown away. They turn a vague feeling, spring seems early this year, into something you can see. And they tie you to one patch of ground: you start to belong to a place by knowing its calendar.
screen: `TRAVELED A GOOD DEAL IN CONCORD.` · `NOTES TURN INTO TABLES.` · `USEFUL TO STRANGERS LATER.` · then, large: `ATTENTION THAT IS KEPT.`

1257.title: Time is a stream
1257.hook: time is but the stream I go a-fishing in (Walden 2)
1257.howItsDone: Some readers take Thoreau's stream as an invitation to spend some time uncounted, sitting beside the hours rather than managing them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was seasons in the journal: when the ice broke and the plants flowered, year after year. Your line was keep records.

Calendars, deadlines, a phone that buzzes on the hour, an app that tells you how long you looked at your phone. On a busy day, time is a thing to manage: spent, saved, wasted, killed. Yesterday Thoreau was keeping careful records of the seasons. Today, in the same book, he picks time up and turns it into something completely different. Not a budget. A stream. And he goes fishing in it.
screen: `SPENT, SAVED, WASTED, KILLED.` → `NOT A BUDGET.` → `A STREAM.`

segments.voice: From Walden's second chapter: "Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in. I drink at it; but while I drink I see the sandy bottom and detect how shallow it is. Its thin current slides away, but eternity remains. I would drink deeper; fish in the sky, whose bottom is pebbly with stars." First, a stream, not a clock. You don't own or spend a stream. You go to it, sit beside it, fish in it, which mostly means waiting. Second, the shallow bottom. Looked at closely, time is thin. The minutes really do slide away, and he doesn't pretend otherwise. Third, but eternity remains. Under the thin current, something doesn't slide. He doesn't define it; he just says it remains. Readers hear different things in that word: God, nature, the timeless, the present moment itself. The sentence leaves room for each of them. Fourth, the sky full of stars. Then he flips the picture: he'd drink deeper, and fish in the sky. The stream becomes the night sky; the shallow bed, a floor of stars. It's a strange image, and it works by feel more than logic: the thin water of hours, opening onto something vast. And it suggests another way to be with time: not always counting it, sometimes sitting beside it, line in the water, letting it run.
screen: `A STREAM, NOT A CLOCK.` · `THE SHALLOW BOTTOM.` · `BUT ETERNITY REMAINS.` · then, large: `FISH IN THE SKY.`

segments.voice: For now, don't count anything, not breaths, not seconds, not how long is left; if your phone is near, turn it face down. Let time go by like water past a bank, noticing the sounds and small shifts in your body without catching any of them. If you find yourself counting, smile and let the count float off downstream.
Time is a stream. Thoreau's picture of time as water he fishes in: shallow, sliding away, and yet with eternity under it. Today's word.
Your line: the stream. You're not spending these minutes; you're sitting beside them. See you tomorrow.

1258.title: At peace with God
1258.hook: dying, asked if he'd made peace with God, he reportedly said he didn't know they had quarreled
1258.howItsDone: Some readers repeat Thoreau's reported deathbed answer as a picture of calm at the end of life, and pair it with his line in Walden that God culminates in the present moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was time is a stream: shallow, sliding away, with eternity beneath it. Your line was the stream.

A sickroom in Concord. Thoreau is very ill, near the end of his life. A relative asks whether he has made his peace with God, and the story goes that he answered, quietly, that he wasn't aware they had ever quarreled. One question, one answer. It's a story that gets retold, and it comes to us secondhand. But it sounds like him. And it opens a real question.
screen: `A SICKROOM IN CONCORD.` → `HAVE YOU MADE YOUR PEACE?` → `I DIDN'T KNOW WE HAD QUARRELED.`

segments.voice: First, the question was a kind one. Asking someone near death whether they've made peace with God can be an act of love. The relative isn't the villain here. Second, the answer. Thoreau doesn't argue about doctrine. He doesn't say yes, and he doesn't say there's no God. He says, in effect, there was never a fight. Whatever he meant by God, he didn't experience the relationship as broken. A whole outlook, folded into one sentence. Third, where that outlook shows up in his books. In Walden he writes, "God himself culminates in the present moment, and will never be more divine in the lapse of all the ages." For Thoreau the sacred wasn't far away and angry. It was here, in this hour, in the pond and the morning. If you meet God, or whatever you call it, in the present moment, there's nothing to patch up later. Another reported answer from those last weeks: asked about the next world, he said, one world at a time. Fourth, what to do with this. Different traditions answer the question of peace with God in their own ways, with confession, repentance, grace, surrender, and they mean deep things by them. Thoreau's line doesn't settle that for anyone. What it offers is a picture of a man who, at the end, seemed unafraid. Not because he'd won an argument, but because he hadn't been having one.
screen: `A KIND QUESTION.` · `THERE WAS NEVER A FIGHT.` · then, large: `GOD IN THE PRESENT MOMENT.` · then: `ONE WORLD AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been quietly at war with: your body, the weather, a noise next door, the pace of your own healing. Don't try to love it; just see whether, for now, you can stop fighting it and breathe beside it, the way you'd sit beside someone you're no longer arguing with. If you pray, you might bring it to God in your own way.

1259.title: Thoreau's limits
1259.hook: critics call him prickly and self-righteous, and his friends sometimes agreed
1259.howItsDone: Some readers of Thoreau hold his sharpness and his goodness together, much as Emerson did in his tribute, naming the prickles without throwing out the man.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was at peace with God: Thoreau's reported answer that he didn't know they had ever quarreled. Your line was no quarrel.

After Thoreau died, Emerson, his friend, wrote a long tribute to him. And right in the middle of the praise, he slips in a sentence that sounds almost like a complaint: "It cost him nothing to say No; indeed he found it much easier than to say Yes." That's a friend talking, not an enemy, in a tribute meant to honor him. After weeks of Thoreau's best lines, today, honestly, the other side.
screen: `EMERSON'S TRIBUTE.` → `EASIER TO SAY NO.` → `THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the no. Refusal came easily to Thoreau. It's the same quality that sent him to jail rather than pay a tax he found unjust, and the one that could make him hard to be around. Second, the elm tree. Emerson passes on a friend's line: I love Henry, "but I cannot like him; and as for taking his arm, I should as soon think of taking the arm of an elm-tree." Love, yes. Ease, no. Upright, rooted, and not soft to lean on. Third, the huckleberry party. Emerson counts it a fault that Thoreau had no ambition. He thought Thoreau had the gifts to lead great public work, and instead, he writes, "Instead of engineering for all America, he was the captain of a huckleberry-party." Some hear a put-down; others hear quiet praise in it: he chose to lead friends to the berries. Fourth, the critics. Some readers since have found Thoreau preachy, scornful of his neighbors, quick to judge how others lived while he lived so differently. Those are fair things to notice; his books do scold. But see what Emerson does: he names the prickles, then keeps praising. The tribute holds both. A person can be hard to like and still be good, and still be worth learning from. That may be what Thoreau's friends teach best about him.
screen: `EASIER TO SAY NO.` · `THE ARM OF AN ELM TREE.` · `CAPTAIN OF A HUCKLEBERRY PARTY.` · then, large: `HARD TO LIKE, STILL GOOD.`

1260.hook: simplicity, wildness, conscience, attention to the small

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Thoreau's limits: Emerson naming how easily Thoreau said no, and loving him anyway. Your line was prickly and good.

A suitcase, and not much room in it. That's roughly where this path is with Thoreau. It has walked through a cabin, a bean field, a pond, a jail cell, a mountain, a shoreline, a journal and a sickroom, and tomorrow it leaves him. Nobody carries a whole writer out the door. So today's question is a packing question: out of everything, what goes in the bag? Here are four things readers pick up from him. You only need one.
screen: `A SMALL SUITCASE.` → `WHAT GOES IN THE BAG?` → `FOUR THINGS, KEEP ONE.`

segments.voice: First, simplicity. In Walden he writes, "Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!" Three times, as if once weren't enough. Fewer things, fewer affairs, so there's room left for a life. Second, wildness. In Walking he writes, "In Wildness is the preservation of the World." Not wilderness only, out there: wildness, the part of the world, and of a person, that hasn't been tamed into usefulness. It was there on Ktaadn, in his cry of contact. Third, conscience. In his essay on civil government: "I think that we should be men first, and subjects afterward." A person before a citizen; conscience before convenience. That's the night in jail, folded into one sentence. Fourth, attention to the small. No single slogan, because it's everywhere: the ice going out on the pond, the line in the journal, a violet's flowering, the stream he fishes in. This week alone, he turned notebooks into seasons and time into water. And Emerson's teasing phrase fits too: the captain of a huckleberry party. Some might call that small. It might be the whole point. Four doors into the same house. Some readers walk in through simplicity, some through the woods, some through protest, some through a notebook. None is the right one. Thoreau wasn't tidy enough to be summed up in one, and his friends would remind you he wasn't easy either. But a person can carry one of these for years.
screen: `SIMPLICITY, SIMPLICITY, SIMPLICITY!` · `IN WILDNESS IS THE PRESERVATION.` · `MEN FIRST, AND SUBJECTS AFTERWARD.` · then, large: `ATTENTION TO THE SMALL.`

segments.voice: Let the four pass by slowly, one per breath: simplicity, wildness, conscience, attention to the small. Notice which one pulls at you, not the one you think you should choose, and let the other three go. Ask what it might look like in an ordinary week: one thing given away, one walk in the rain, one honest no, one line in a notebook.
What to keep from Thoreau. Simplicity, wildness, conscience, attention to the small: four doors, and you only need one. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT TO KEEP FROM THOREAU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep one. One door is enough to get into the house. I'll be here tomorrow.

Moving out to a cabin in the woods, since that's the only real way to live as he did.
Protest, since his essay on conscience is the one part of him that really matters.
